title: Ang 691–695: the Bhagats' aartis
tomorrow: can the bravest person in the room admit they're scared?

lines: A GROCERY LIST IN YOUR PHONE.
cards: Somewhere in your notes app there's probably a grocery list: lentils, flour, oil, the thing you forgot last time. Turn to ang 695 of the Guru Granth Sahib and there's nearly that list, inside a hymn.
Dhanna, a farmer in tradition, sings to God, and asks for lentils, flour and ghee. Then shoes, good clothes, grain, a cow, a fine horse. In scripture.
So here's the puzzle: why does a holy book keep a shopping list?

teach.b: These pages close Dhanasri with the Bhagats, saints from outside the line of the Gurus: Kabir, Namdev, Ravidas and others. Several of them sing an aarti, the song of worship sung as lamps are waved.
A few days ago, Guru Nanak made the whole sky the aarti platter. Here the Bhagats bring it close.
Ravidas, on ang 694: your Name is my aarti and my bath. Sain, a barber in tradition: lamps, incense and ghee for the aarti; I'm a sacrifice to you.
Pipa, a king in tradition who gave up his throne: the body itself is the temple, the god and the pilgrim; whatever is in the universe is in the body, and whoever searches finds it. Then Dhanna.
Lord, this is your aarti; you set right the affairs of those who worship you. And then the list, so that, as he says, the heart stays glad. So, the puzzle.
The Granth doesn't keep Dhanna's list by accident. It keeps it beside Ravidas and Pipa, as an aarti in its own right. Worship doesn't have to sound grand.
A farmer's real needs, said straight to God, count. Sikhs still pray that way: Ardas, the standing prayer, can name a meal, a journey, someone who's ill.

how: The Bhagats' aartis, among them Ravidas's 'your Name is my aarti' and Sain's, are sung in many gurdwaras in the evening, and Sikhs' Ardas often names ordinary needs and occasions.

games.q: the Bhagats' aartis — tap the pairs.
p: lamps and incense: I'm a sacrifice

s: the Guru Granth Sahib holds only hymns by the Sikh Gurus
Bhagats such as Kabir, Ravidas, Sain, Pipa and Dhanna have hymns here too.
Dhanna's aarti asks God for lentils, flour and ghee
and shoes, clothes, grain, a cow and a horse, so his heart stays glad (ang 695).
Pipa says the temple you need is far away
Pipa says the body is the temple; whoever searches finds it.

games.q: before a long drive, your grandmother's prayer is: let the car start and the roads be clear. your cousin says real prayers should be about bigger things. what fits ang 695?
o: your cousin's right: scripture keeps prayer for the soul alone.
keep it private; out loud, prayer should sound more formal.
a plain need said honestly is worship too; the Granth keeps Dhanna's.
games.why: Dhanna's aarti asks for lentils, flour, ghee and shoes, and the Granth keeps it beside Ravidas and Pipa. plain prayers count.

practice: Say one plain need out loud, in ordinary words, the way Dhanna did: a good night's sleep, the rent, a friend who feels better soon. If you pray, that's a prayer; if not, it's still worth hearing yourself say it.
Then let the sit hold the quiet that comes after.

carryVoice: Plain prayers: an aarti can be lentils and ghee, said straight, with a glad heart. That's day fifteen twenty-eight, and that's the list.
